headline: Local Band Plays First Gig to Audience of Three, Calls It 'Intimate' and 'Exactly What We Wanted'
summary: Newly formed group Static Voltage performed 45-minute set at The Underground to crowd consisting entirely of band members' relatives.
content:
Local four-piece Static Voltage took the stage at The Underground last Friday night for their debut performance, delivering a 45-minute set of original alternative rock to an audience of three—all of whom shared DNA with at least one band member.

"We're really focusing on building a grassroots fanbase," said lead guitarist and vocalist Tyler Moss, 24, after the show. "And what's more grassroots than your mom, your aunt, and your drummer's grandmother?"

The audience—Moss's mother Linda, his aunt Patricia, and drummer Kevin Okonkwo's grandmother Beatrice—occupied a table near the front of the venue, which can hold approximately 150 people. They applauded enthusiastically after each song.

"I couldn't hear most of it because it was very loud," admitted Beatrice Okonkwo, 78. "But Kevin looked so happy up there. I told him I'd come to his first show and I meant it."

The Underground's booking manager, who goes by the name Mars, noted that small crowds are common for debut acts. "Everyone starts somewhere," Mars said. "I've seen bands play to empty rooms. Three supportive family members is actually above average for a first gig."

Static Voltage performed eight original songs, including "Digital Heartbreak," "Screaming into the Algorithm," and a seven-minute closing number called "Existential Traffic" that featured an extended bass solo.

"The acoustics in here are incredible," said bassist Jordan Webb. "You could really hear every note. Probably because there wasn't a lot of crowd noise to compete with."

The band has already booked a second show for next month. Moss confirmed that his father, who couldn't attend Friday's performance due to a work conflict, has "committed to being there."

"We're projecting an audience of four," Moss said. "Maybe five if my sister can get off work. Growth is growth."
author: Ellen Park, Arts & Culture
